Southeast DOT Lighting Intelligence

Eight state DOTs, one picture: where the money is, where the lighting is, who pays for it, who decides, and who to call.

Alternative delivery — the lighting the bid tabulations cannot seedesign-build · progressive design-build · CM/GC · P3 · who designs the lighting · what is ahead

Every dollar of lighting on this site so far came from a low-bid tabulation. Design-build, progressive design-build, CM/GC and P3 contracts publish none: the agency awards one price to a team and the lighting sits inside it. This section lists every such contract the eight agencies have awarded or advertised since 2023, quotes what each published scope says about lighting, and states who designs the lighting on that kind of job in each state — because on a design-build the specification decision is made by whoever holds the lighting design, before any bid.

The money, state by statewhat each figure is · who appropriates · the plan · the split · who commits · a lighting line?

The programme-size figure on the map and the cards is each state's own top line, restated from the instrument that carries it: six are enacted appropriations for the current year, South Carolina's is the agency's adopted programme budget (its FY 2026-27 appropriation is ratified with vetoes pending), Tennessee's is the Work Program the Department calls its budget. Seven fiscal years start on July 1; Alabama's starts October 1; South Carolina's figure is a year older than the rest. What each includes differs (federal money is inside six of them and outside North Carolina's), and none carries a construction lighting line. They are shown for scale, never blended and never used as a denominator; the lighting money is read from the lettings, the same way in all eight states.

The territory at a glance

One card per state: how big the programme is, who owns the light and who buys it, what is programmed, and where the bid record stands. Every line is measured or stated by the agency itself; a state that has not been read says so. Open a card for the full model.

What changed — this record against its last snapshotcomputed at open · the snapshot history

Every build leaves a digest of the record behind; the page recomputes the same digest when it opens and lists the difference — new reads, lighting contracts, awards confirmed, programme moves, contacts, lists, sources — and any layer whose source should have moved by now. Computed, never typed.

Programmed lighting — the call list across the territorylighting-only projects, in construction-year order · counted, never valued

Every project in the four states that publish a searchable programme whose scope is lighting and nothing else, in construction-year order. These are the contracts that have not been let yet — the earliest call list the public record can produce. Counted, never valued: a cost is the whole project's programmed cost as the agency prints it, or absent where the agency publishes none.

Eight-state money board — reported budget, or the lighting ladderfour measures, never blended · constant dollars

One chart, four measures, never blended. Reported budget is each DOT's own top line — different budget objects, labelled by basis. The other three are the lighting ladder from the Phase 4 overlay: what each agency has programmed as lighting-only projects, what it let as lighting in the twelve months read, and what of that is awarded. Select a bar to open the state's full model.

Measure

Permanent rule: lighting dollars come from L1/L2 contracts and awarded lighting pay items — never a fixed percentage of a DOT budget. Geographic shading uses an official allocation only where the state publishes one; otherwise it shows identified programmed project value and is labeled accordingly.

The territory calendar — what lets next, and when lighting is due backevery dated thing ahead, with its basis

Every dated thing ahead, on one list: each agency's next lettings (its own schedule first, Bid Express's nine-agency calendar second), the programmed lighting-only projects the agencies have themselves dated, and the rebids that recurring contracts' own titles imply. The basis sits on every row — a schedule, an observed pattern, a programme year or an inference — because a date without its basis is a guess dressed up.

Who owns the light — the regulatory environment, state by statewho owns, when the DOT pays, who signs, what starts a sale

Whether lighting can appear in a DOT contract at all is decided by who owns the asset, when the DOT ever pays, who signs off, and what starts a sale — and that differs at the root from state to state. Each row is built only from that state's own published record; the detail, with sources, is on the state's page.

Method — the rules, what is built, and what comes nextthe layer model · integrity rules · what a figure means

The map is the interface; the intelligence engine is the product. This page is how it is made: the six rules every figure obeys, the twelve layers and which states carry them, the bid record each state publishes, and the roadmap.

What is built, state by statethe coverage matrix · seven transferable layers, five bid-derived

The platform is twelve layers. Seven transfer to any state DOT and need no bid data at all; five are derived from reading bid tabulations and are state-specific by construction. This matrix is computed from the data each state actually carries — it cannot claim a layer the page does not have.

Freshness — how old each layer is, and when its source should moveas-of · next expected · the award sweep

Phase 9, briefing-side: every layer of every state states its own age and its next expected date from the catalogue's cadences, reads fresh, due or STALE against today's date, and the build refuses a STALE layer. Below it, the award sweep — every lighting contract still apparent and the date its agency's award artifact should exist.

Whose product qualifies — the eight states on one pagelists, Cooper's status, the specification, the gate

Phase 7, public record only: for each agency, whether a list of approved luminaires or poles exists and who is on it, whether Cooper Lighting Solutions is, how the specification is written, and who approves a product. It is a qualification picture — where the door is open and who is standing in it — never a share picture; the tabulations name classes, not brands, and no state publishes what was installed.

Recurrence — what comes round, read from the agencies' own titlesthe register · the lighting cadence · next lettings

Phase 6 reads recurrence the only way one year of record allows: by type. A contract is recurring when the agency's own title says so — on-call, as-needed, annual, a programme at various locations or statewide, an emergency letting, or a term titled by fiscal year — and a rebid is inferred only where the title carries its term. The lighting cadence is the year's observed pattern of standalone lighting contracts, stated as one year's pattern. Nothing here predicts; it records what the agency said and when it said it, and the second year turns type into rate.

The people ledger — who is still who, computed todaythe SLA · the ledger · export and import

Phase 5 makes contact staleness a computed fact rather than a discovery mid-phone-call: every person on every state page carries the date the record last saw them — the directory read, or a verification logged by whoever spoke to them — and reads active, stale or UNKNOWN against that date each time the page opens. The local and utility owners who hold the light off the DOT's freeways are carried as records of their own.

The financial overlay — three measurements of the same money, and what is never comparedprogrammed · let · awarded · the five rules

Phase 4 puts the lighting money on one scale at three moments — programmed (the agency's own lighting-only projects, at its year-of-expenditure cost), let (lighting identified at the low bidder over the twelve months read) and awarded (confirmed by the agency's award artifact) — and states two things about every figure: its basis, and whether it has been restated in one quarter's money.

The accuracy pass — what is provisional in the lighting numbers, and the data that will settle itthe threshold table · the dictionaries · the owner's marks

The dollars on every state page are read line by line and reconciled; what is ours, not the agency's, is the rule that makes a contract a lighting contract (one lighting-specific pay item, any size), the 75 % line between a standalone lighting contract (L1) and lighting inside a larger job (L2), and the single hardware bucket. This section shows what those rules do to the numbers, so the owner can set a commercial definition from the data rather than from a guess.

The bid record — eight states against one checklisttabs, dictionary, award artifact, completeness anchor

Before a state's lettings can be read for lighting at item level, four things must exist in public: itemised bid tabulations for every bidder, a pay-item scheme with a lighting section, an award artifact, and a printed contract total per bidder to reconcile against. This is the catalogue of what each DOT publishes — assembled September 3–4, 2026 from the agencies' own artifacts, and cited state by state. It is not a lighting finding by itself: the lighting findings are on the state pages of the states that have been read at item level (the coverage matrix below shows which).

The rules this runs onthe integrity rules, in one place

Six rules decide what this platform is allowed to say — because a number that cannot be defended in front of a customer is worse than no number at all.

1
No manufactured geography. A territory total is the identified, programmed value of projects located there — never a district's share of a state budget.
2
No manufactured lighting dollars. Lighting money comes from priced Division 14 pay items in real contracts, never a percentage of a DOT budget. Scope that carries no separable price never enters a dollar total.
3
Apparent is not awarded. A low bid stays apparent until the Board's own record says the contract was awarded. The two are shown differently and never summed together.
4
No manufactured manufacturer share. Meeting a specification is not the same as being installed. Until submittal or acceptance evidence exists the manufacturer is UNKNOWN — as it is for every contract here today.
5
No manufactured people. A vacancy stays vacant, and an email is never guessed from a naming pattern even an obvious one.
6
Every figure traces to a numbered source, and anything not yet read says so in plain words rather than being left blank or quietly rounded to zero.

How evidence is graded

Lighting scope (contract level)

  • L1Standalone lighting contract
    Full award counts as confirmed lighting dollars when substantially lighting.
  • L2Quantified lighting items
    Awarded lighting pay items summed inside a larger contract.
  • L3Explicit but inseparable
    Lighting scope confirmed; dollars unknown. Never enters confirmed totals.
  • L4Potential pipeline
    Forecast or plan-stage possibility. Counted, not valued.

Manufacturer evidence — what the public record shows

  • M1Confirmed installed
    As-built, inspection, or materials-acceptance record.
  • M2Purchased / approved for installation
    Submittal approved or purchase documented for a project.
  • M3Specified or approved equal
    Named in project plans or specifications.
  • M4QPL-eligible only
    Eligibility is never treated as installation.
  • M5Unknown
    A valid published state. No backfilling.

Competition. Plan holders are not bidders; apparent low is not final award; incomplete bidder archives carry a completeness flag before any comparative metric is published.

People. Names, roles, and verification dates are versioned. A vacancy or stale directory entry stays UNKNOWN — never silently backfilled.

Finance. Appropriation, allocation, obligation, encumbrance, expenditure, and carry-forward are distinct fields. Carry-forward is a stock snapshot, never added across years.

Product roadmapwhere the roadmap stands · the nine phases

Ten phases in three horizons. Each phase ships something usable on its own and inherits the integrity rules — nothing manufactured, every figure traceable.

Steering decision, September 4 2026 — the bid layer reopens, designed from eight states. The August 31 pause did its job: every state is modeled on the seven transferable layers, so the bid method is now being rebuilt from eight states’ evidence rather than one state’s habits. build 3.8 (September 4) was the catalogue — each DOT’s bid tabulations, item-code scheme, award artifact and reconciliation anchor checked against one four-item list, on the Overview and on every state page — and the universal contract record every future read is captured to: bidders from the award artifact, a class, the lighting total split into hardware, electrical infrastructure and work, quantities by class, and every bidder’s unit price on every lighting line. Reading order followed the evidence — Kentucky first (state-owned, the highest expected rate), Arkansas second as the control (request state, the lowest) — and the other five each got a full year rather than a sample, because the direct reads were fast once the network opened: Georgia, Alabama, South Carolina, Tennessee and Mississippi followed between September 4 and 5. The bid layer is an evidence and quantities layer, never a market-size instrument; North Carolina’s read stays as the reference adapter.

The twelve layers, and which ones travel

Seven of the twelve layers need no bid data at all. They are what a second state can be stood up from, and they answer the sales questions the public record can answer on its own — where the money is, who pays, who decides, what is coming, and who to call.

Since build 2.1 this table is enforced rather than described: the coverage matrix on the Overview is computed from the data each state actually carries, and the build fails if an absent layer renders anything but UNKNOWN. The bid-derived layers are what produce the dollar figures on a state page that has been read — all eight states since build 3.17. Those numbers are real and sourced; they are simply not the cheapest thing to reproduce eight times, and nothing else in the model depends on them.

Horizon 2 — Scale it
  1. 3

    Eight-state rollout on the transferable layerscomplete — all eight states modeled and read at item level, build 3.18 · accuracy pass 3.20 · NC Divisions 3.21

    Ships: each state's ownership and funding model, decision-maker, pipeline and contacts — built from that state's own published record, with the bid model paused until three states can be compared. All eight states are now modeled — four ownership shapes: North Carolina decides by policy (a warrant test and a standing committee); Alabama, Mississippi and Arkansas are distributed (case-by-case — city by city in Alabama, split at the city line by statute in Mississippi under its elected commission, and by local request in Arkansas, where ARDOT says on the record that the city keeps the lights on); Tennessee, Georgia and South Carolina are two-key (a state approval plus a local owner — a warrant in Tennessee, a signed commitment in Georgia, a photometric approval and encroachment permit in South Carolina); and Kentucky is state-owned — KYTC installs and maintains its own lighting, with the project list enacted by the General Assembly as law.

    Milestones: 3.1 Alabama ✓ · 3.2 Tennessee ✓ · 3.3 Georgia ✓ — the model's first standing annual DOT lighting program · 3.4 Mississippi ✓ — the model's first elected DOT governance · 3.5 Kentucky ✓ — the first state-owned lighting model, with a pipeline read straight out of an enacted statute · 3.6 South Carolina ✓ — the permit state, whose lighting rules were transcribed from its own right-of-way manuals · 3.7 Arkansas ✓ — the request state, and the territory is complete · 3.8 the bid catalogue ✓ — eight states against one four-item checklist, the universal contract record, and a letting-calendar strip on every state page · 3.9 Georgia ✓ (fourteen lettings) · 3.10 Kentucky ✓ (twelve) · 3.11 Arkansas ✓ (the control read, matched to ARDOT's own price census) · 3.12 Alabama ✓ · 3.13 competition ✓ and 3.13a the review · 3.14 map modes and the price book ✓ · 3.15 South Carolina ✓ · 3.16 Tennessee ✓ · 3.17 Mississippi ✓ — all eight at item level · 3.18 the empty bubbles ✓ — pipeline for four states, Alabama's awards. · 3.20 the accuracy pass, data side ✓ — hardware sub-split, the threshold table, the dictionaries on one page. · 3.19 the NC Division channel ✓ and the NC price book (build 3.21) — all 14 Divisions at contract level, North Carolina a full peer of the other seven. Remaining in the phase: the owner's threshold and dictionary decisions.

    Done when: every state's page explains who owns, funds and approves lighting from its own sources, and no comparative metric publishes across incompatible denominators. — Met, and then some: every state also carries a full letting year read at item level, which was not in the phase's original scope.
